body:
FOUND while building T79 (the artifact host), 2026-07-25, from a rail that would not go green for a reason that turned out not to be T79's.

THE HEADLINE, and it is the second half rather than the first: A MALFORMED `mutations` PAYLOAD CAN TAKE `writable` DOWN WITH IT, so a store BOOTS BELIEVING IT IS IMMUTABLE-BY-DEFAULT while the operator explicitly declared a write surface. That is a silent failure in the WRONG DIRECTION on the write surface — not 'a write is refused that should have landed' (loud, recoverable, a bug report) but 'the operator's declaration evaporated and the store looks correctly locked down'. §21's immutable-by-default is a deny-by-default posture, which means its failure mode is indistinguishable from its intended state. Nobody files a bug about a door that is closed.

MEASURED, on a genesis-borne registration:
  registrations: [{ hyperschema: PLANT, schema: PLANT_POLICY, roots: [FERN],
                    writable: ["height", "tag"],
                    mutations: { water: { pointers: [{ role: "value", context: "watered", value: true }] } } }]
  → the BINDING DELTA carries both, verified in the bytes:
      { role: "mutations", target: { kind: "primitive", value: "{\"water\":{...}}" } }
      { role: "writable",  target: { kind: "primitive", value: "[\"height\",\"tag\"]" } }
  → `gw.registered.find(r => lensOf(r) === "Plant")` answers `{ writable: undefined, mutations: {} }`.
Drop the `mutations` key from the same spec and `writable` comes back as `['height','tag']`. So the presence of a malformed template payload is what loses the writable list.

THE TEMPLATE WAS MALFORMED, and that part is correct behavior: `parseClaimTemplates` requires EXACTLY ONE of `at`/`value` per pointer, and `context` belongs to an `at` pointer — so `{ role, context, value }` is refused. The right shape is `{ pointers: [{ role: "value", value: true }] }`. The refusal is not the defect; WHAT ELSE THE REFUSAL COSTS is.

WHERE TO LOOK. `readRegistrations`' candidate reader (src/gateway/registration.ts, around the `mutations` / `writable` / `resolvers` reads) is written to drop each payload QUIETLY and INDEPENDENTLY — 'a malformed template payload is dropped QUIETLY (the schema still binds; the surface just lacks the mutation) — the loud refusal belongs to publish, not replay'. Read alone, each of the three reads looks correct. The measurement says they are not independent in practice, so the first thing this ticket owes is finding out WHY: either something upstream of the reader (a shared parse, an early `continue`, the surviving-candidate grouping) abandons the rest of the extras block, or `assembleGenesis` is not carrying what the delta appears to carry. Do not assume the reader; measure it.

AND THE DOCTRINE QUESTION UNDERNEATH, which is the part worth Myk's eye: quiet-drop-on-replay is the right instinct for a RESOLVER (the field falls back to its Policy value — a narrower reading, and a reader can see it) and it is the wrong instinct for `writable`, because dropping it does not narrow a reading, it silently REVOKES a declared authority. The registration reader's comment even says the fallback leaves 'the schema permissive rather than refusing to bind' — which is the opposite of what §21's flip made true. Immutable-by-default means the absent case is the LOCKED case, so 'quietly absent' and 'deliberately locked' are the same bytes to every downstream reader.

WHAT A FIX MIGHT BE (not decided — this is P0):
  (a) Make the three reads genuinely independent, so a bad template costs only the template. Necessary either way.
  (b) Refuse the BINDING rather than drop a field, when the payload that fails to parse is one whose absence changes an AUTHORITY rather than a reading. A registration that cannot be read faithfully binds nothing, which is the fail-closed direction and the one §7 already takes elsewhere.
  (c) Make it visible: `store health` / `loam store` should be able to say 'this binding carries an unreadable payload', because today the only evidence is a write that mysteriously refuses.
(b) needs care: a store that boots today would stop binding, so it is a behavior change with a migration question attached.

RAILS THIS TICKET OWES, both levels, and note the second is the one that matters:
  - DELTA: a genesis-borne registration's binding carries `mutations` AND `writable`, asserted over the delta's pointers (this already holds today).
  - OBJECT: the SURFACE the gateway serves from it names the same writable set — `gw.registered`'s `writable`, and a `/graphql` mutation on a declared field SUCCEEDING. The delta assertion alone is exactly what cannot see this bug: the bytes are right and the reading is wrong, which is T15/T38's shape one layer up.
  - And the two-sided form: a malformed `mutations` costs the TEMPLATES and a named live bystander (`writable`) SURVIVES.

WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED IN T79. T79's criterion 32 is about the capability statement's DERIVATION, which is a pure function of (registration, binding, manifest); it was railed by calling that function directly, and the test header says so. Fixing a registration-reader defect inside a publication-surface ticket would have widened T79 past its wedge and buried a wrong-direction write-surface bug in a PR about artifacts. It is named here instead.

EVIDENCE: test/gateway/artifact-capability-text.test.ts (the header records the gap and why the derivation is railed directly); src/gateway/registration.ts (`parseClaimTemplates`, and the candidate reader's three quiet-drop branches); src/gateway/genesis.ts (`assembleGenesis`, which passes `reg.mutations` and `reg.writable` through to `registrationDeltaClaims`).
title: A malformed claim template silently takes `writable` with it — a store can boot believing it is immutable-by-default while the operator declared a write surface
